2.1 Database Management Systems, Data Warehousing and Big

What is Data Management?
Definition: Data management is the process of collecting, storing, 
organizing, protecting, and maintaining an organization's data so that it 
is accurate, available, and usable for business operations and decision￾making.
• Good data management ensures data quality, security, accessibility, 
and compliance with regulations (e.g., data privacy laws).
• Poor data management leads to duplicate, inconsistent, or unreliable 
data, which weakens business decisions.
Database Management System (DBMS)
• Definition: A Database Management System (DBMS) is software 
that allows organizations to create, store, organize, retrieve, and 
manage data in an efficient, secure, and reliable way.
• A DBMS acts as an interface between the user/application and the 
physical database, so users do not need to know how data is actually 
stored on disk.
• It supports data creation, insertion, updation, deletion, and querying 
using languages such as SQL (Structured Query Language).
• Key functions of a DBMS: 
◦ Data storage, retrieval, and update.
◦ Enforcing data integrity and consistency rules (constraints, keys, 
relationships).
◦ Providing security through authentication, authorization, and 
access control.
◦ Supporting concurrent multi-user access without conflicts 
(concurrency control).

ACID Properties of a DBMS Transaction
• Atomicity: A transaction is treated as a single, indivisible unit — it 
either completes fully or not at all.
• Consistency: A transaction takes the database from one valid state 
to another, preserving all defined rules.
• Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other; 
each executes as if it were alone.
• Durability: Once a transaction is committed, its changes are 
permanent, even after a system failure.

According to Bill Inmon, a data warehouse has four defining 
characteristics:
• Subject-oriented – organized around key business subjects such as 
sales, customers, or products rather than around applications.
• Integrated – data from different sources is made consistent in 
naming, format, and units.
• Time-variant – data is stored with a time dimension, allowing trend 
and historical analysis.
• Non-volatile – once data enters the warehouse, it is not changed or 
deleted; it is only added to.
Fig 2.1: Three-tier Data Warehouse Architecture — data flows from 
operational sources through ETL into a central warehouse, and finally 
into subject-specific data marts used by end users.

ETL Process (Extract, Transform, Load)
• Extract: Data is collected/pulled from various heterogeneous source 
systems such as operational databases, flat files, and external feeds.
• Transform: Extracted data is cleaned, validated, standardized (e.g., 
date formats, currency units), de-duplicated, and converted into a 
consistent format suitable for analysis.
• Load: The transformed data is loaded into the central data 
warehouse (or data marts) for querying and reporting. Loading may 
be a full load (first time) or incremental load (only new/changed 
records).

Data Warehouse Schemas
• Star Schema: A central fact table (containing measurable, 
quantitative business data such as sales amount) is connected 
directly to multiple dimension tables (such as product, customer, 
time, and store) that provide descriptive context.
• Snowflake Schema: An extension of the star schema where 
dimension tables are further normalized into sub-dimension tables, 
reducing redundancy but increasing query complexity.
Fig 2.2: Star Schema — a central Sales Fact table linked to Product, 
Customer, Time, and Store dimension tables.
Data Marts
• Definition: A Data Mart is a smaller, specialized subset of a data 
warehouse that is focused on the needs of a specific business unit or 
department, such as Sales, Finance, or HR.

• Data marts are faster to build and query than a full data warehouse 
because they hold a limited, focused dataset.
• Dependent data mart: Sources its data directly from the central 
data warehouse (top-down approach).
• Independent data mart: Built directly from operational source 
systems without going through a central warehouse (bottom-up 
approach).
• Hybrid data mart: Combines inputs from both the central 
warehouse and additional local operational sources.
Example: A Sales Data Mart may contain only sales-related facts 
(revenue, units sold, region) drawn from the larger enterprise warehouse, 
allowing the sales team to analyze performance quickly without 
querying the entire warehouse.
Big Data Concepts
• Definition: Big Data refers to extremely large, complex, and fast￾growing datasets that traditional data-processing software and 
databases cannot efficiently capture, store, manage, or analyze.
Fig 2.3: The 5 V's of Big Data — Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, 
and Value.

• Volume: The sheer scale of data generated every day — from 
terabytes to zettabytes — by social media, sensors, transactions, and 
devices.
• Velocity: The speed at which new data is generated and must be 
processed, often in real time (e.g., stock trades, IoT sensor streams, 
UPI transactions).
• Variety: Data exists in structured (tables), semi-structured (XML, 
JSON), and unstructured (images, video, social posts) forms.
• Veracity: The trustworthiness, accuracy, and quality of the data —
noisy, incomplete, or biased data reduces the value of analysis.
• Value: The ultimate business usefulness that can be extracted from 
the data through analytics — data is only "big" data if it can be 
turned into insight.
Big Data Technologies
• Hadoop: An open-source framework that allows distributed storage 
(HDFS) and processing (MapReduce) of very large datasets across 
clusters of commodity computers.
• Apache Spark: An in-memory, distributed data-processing engine 
that is significantly faster than traditional MapReduce for iterative 
analytics and machine learning.
• NoSQL databases: Databases such as MongoDB and Cassandra 
designed to handle unstructured or semi-structured Big Data at scale.
Case studies: Amazon analyzes clickstream and purchase data at
massive scale to power personalized product recommendations; Netflix 
processes viewing data across hundreds of millions of users worldwide 
to personalize content and design new shows; Indian digital enterprises 
such as UPI-based payment platforms process billions of real-time 
transactions daily, requiring high-velocity Big Data infrastructure.

Before understanding BI, it helps to see how raw facts are progressively 
refined into business wisdom:
Fig 2.4: The DIKW Pyramid — Data, Information, Knowledge, and 
Wisdom.
• Data: Raw, unprocessed facts and figures (e.g., a list of transaction 
amounts).
• Information: Data that has been organized and given context (e.g., 
total sales per month).
• Knowledge: Understanding the patterns and relationships within 
information (e.g., sales peak every festive season).
• Wisdom: Applying knowledge with judgement to make sound 
decisions (e.g., increasing festive-season inventory in advance).
Business Intelligence (BI)
• Definition: Business Intelligence refers to the technologies, 
applications, and practices used to collect, integrate, analyze, and 
present business data to support better organizational decision￾making.
• BI converts raw operational data into meaningful information 
through reporting, dashboards, and analysis.
• Goal: help managers and executives make faster, fact-based 
decisions instead of relying on intuition alone.

• Roll-up: Aggregates data by climbing up a concept hierarchy (e.g., 
summarizing sales from city level to state level).
• Drill-down: The reverse of roll-up — breaks summarized data into 
finer detail (e.g., yearly sales broken into monthly sales).
• Slice: Selects a single value for one dimension, creating a sub-cube 
(e.g., sales for only the year 2025).
• Dice: Selects a sub-cube by specifying values for two or more 
dimensions (e.g., sales for "Electronics" in "West Region" during 
"Q1").
• Pivot (Rotate): Rotates the data axes to view the cube from a 
different perspective, useful for cross-tabulation.

scatter plots, and geographic maps.

• Classification: Assigns data into predefined categories (e.g.,

• Clustering: Groups similar data points together without predefined 
labels (e.g., segmenting customers by purchase behavior).
• Association rule mining: Finds relationships between variables 
(e.g., "customers who buy bread also buy butter" — market basket 
analysis).
• Regression: Predicts a continuous numeric value based on other 
variables (e.g., predicting next month's revenue).
• Anomaly/outlier detection: Identifies unusual data points that 
differ significantly from the rest (e.g., detecting fraudulent 
transactions).

Fig 2.9: Types of Business Analytics — Descriptive, Diagnostic, 
Predictive, and Prescriptive.
• Descriptive analytics: Summarizes historical data to explain "what 
happened" (e.g., last quarter's sales report).
• Diagnostic analytics: Examines data to understand "why it 
happened" (e.g., root-cause analysis of a sales drop).
• Predictive analytics: Uses statistical models and machine learning 
on historical data to forecast "what is likely to happen" (e.g., 
predicting customer churn or demand).
• Prescriptive analytics: Recommends specific actions — "what 
should be done" — often using optimization and AI techniques (e.g., 
dynamic pricing recommendations).
Common predictive-analytics techniques include regression analysis, 
decision trees, time-series forecasting, and neural networks. These are 
widely used for demand forecasting, credit-risk scoring, churn 
prediction, and predictive maintenance in manufacturing.
